```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

In multisite trials the size of a site's effect is often related to the
precision of its estimate, for example when small sites show larger effects.
`sim_multisite()` generates site effects and standard errors independently
unless the design sets the `dependence` argument. The argument offers three
methods. The sections below compare them, show how to check the correlation
in the simulated data, and cover designs with a site-level covariate and a
user-supplied dependence function.

## Three methods

The dependence step runs after the site effects and the standard errors have
been generated and before the estimates are drawn. It keeps every value and
changes only which site has which standard error. The standard errors,
together with their site sizes, are reassigned among the sites until effects
and standard errors are related as the design asks. A positive target gives
the larger standard errors to the sites with the larger effects, and a
negative target gives them the smaller ones. `sim_meta()` takes the same
arguments.

| `dependence` | Target argument | Meaning of the target |
|--------------|-----------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `"rank"` | `rank_corr` | Spearman correlation between site effects and standard errors in the simulated data |
| `"copula"` | `pearson_corr` | correlation between the normal scores of the site effects and the latent scores that order the standard errors |
| `"hybrid"` | `rank_corr` | as for `"rank"` |

The examples use 100 sites and the defaults for all other design arguments.
The first data set has no dependence and serves as the comparison.

```{r none}
dat_none <- sim_multisite(J = 100, seed = 1)
dat_none
```

`vignette("multisiteDGP")` explains the header and the columns. The third
header line sets the target of 0.000 against the rank correlation in these 100
sites, which is 0.093 by chance.

### The rank method

`dependence = "rank"` starts from the standard errors as generated, or from
standard errors sorted by effect if that order is closer to the target. It
then exchanges the standard errors of two sites at a time, each time the pair
that brings the Spearman correlation closest to `rank_corr`. It stops within
`tol` of the target (0.02 by default) and uses no random numbers.

```{r rank}
dat_rank <- sim_multisite(
  J = 100, dependence = "rank", rank_corr = 0.4, seed = 1
)
print(dat_rank, n = 3)
```

The header shows a realized rank correlation of 0.400. The three rows printed
are identical to the first three of `dat_none`, because the method stopped
after a few exchanges.

### The copula method

`dependence = "copula"` draws for each site a latent score that has
correlation `pearson_corr` with the normal score of its effect (the standard
normal quantile that corresponds to the effect's rank). The site with the
lowest score receives the smallest standard error, the next lowest the next
smallest, and so on. This pairing of effects and standard errors is a draw
from a Gaussian copula. When neither the effects nor the standard errors have
tied values, the rank correlation in the data varies around a value close to
`pearson_corr` (0.385 for 0.4).

```{r copula}
dat_copula <- sim_multisite(
  J = 100, dependence = "copula", pearson_corr = 0.4, seed = 1
)
print(dat_copula, n = 3)
```

The rank correlation line shows no target, because the copula method sets the
correlation of the latent scores and not the rank correlation of the data. The
realized value is 0.328. The standard errors in all three rows differ from
those in `dat_none`.

### The hybrid method

`dependence = "hybrid"` combines the two. It draws a copula pairing with the
latent correlation that corresponds to `rank_corr`. It then exchanges standard
errors as the rank method does until the rank correlation is within `tol` of
the target.

```{r hybrid}
dat_hybrid <- sim_multisite(
  J = 100, dependence = "hybrid", rank_corr = 0.4, seed = 1
)
print(dat_hybrid, n = 3)
```

The realized rank correlation is 0.400, as with the rank method, and the
standard errors are reassigned throughout, as with the copula method.

### Comparison of the methods

The three data sets can be compared with `dat_none` site by site.

```{r comparison}
dats <- list(rank = dat_rank, copula = dat_copula, hybrid = dat_hybrid)
sapply(dats, function(x) sum(x$se_j != dat_none$se_j))
sapply(dats, function(x) identical(sort(x$se_j), sort(dat_none$se_j)))
sapply(dats, function(x) identical(x$tau_j, dat_none$tau_j))
```

The first result counts the sites whose standard error differs from
`dat_none`: 10 under the rank method, 100 and 99 under the other two. The
second and third results show what no method changes. The sorted standard
errors equal those of `dat_none`, and so do the site effects, site by site.
Only the pairing differs, which is why all four headers show the same
`sigma_tau` and the same informativeness.

```{r methods, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Filled points are the sites whose standard error differs from the data without dependence: 10 under the rank method, nearly all under the other two."}
library(ggplot2)
panels <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dats, as.data.frame))
panels$method <- factor(rep(names(dats), each = 100), levels = names(dats))
panels$reassigned <- panels$se_j != rep(dat_none$se_j, 3)
ggplot(panels, aes(tau_j, se_j, shape = reassigned)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16)) +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  labs(x = "Site effect", y = "Standard error", shape = "Reassigned") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Each panel shows a loose upward cloud, as a rank correlation near 0.4 implies.
The ten filled points in the left panel are sites with lower effects that
received smaller standard errors and sites with higher effects that received
larger ones. Exchanges among these ten sites were enough to reach the target.
In the other two panels the dependence runs through all sites.

One data set per method does not show how the realized correlation behaves
over repeated simulations. The next example simulates 100 data sets with the
copula method and 100 with the hybrid method.

```{r repeated}
realized <- function(seed, ...) {
  realized_rank_corr(sim_multisite(J = 100, ..., seed = seed))
}
r_copula <- sapply(1:100, realized, dependence = "copula", pearson_corr = 0.4)
r_hybrid <- sapply(1:100, realized, dependence = "hybrid", rank_corr = 0.4)
round(rbind(copula = summary(r_copula), hybrid = summary(r_hybrid)), 3)
```

`realized_rank_corr()` returns the rank correlation of one data set. Under the
copula method it ranges from 0.137 to 0.569 over the 100 seeds, with a mean of
0.394. Under the hybrid method it stays between 0.383 and 0.418, within `tol`
of the target. The rank method stops by the same rule and behaves like the
hybrid method in this respect. Both warn when a search ends further than `tol`
from the target.

## Choosing a method

Use `"hybrid"` unless there is a reason to prefer another method. With a
target other than 0 it returns a rank correlation within `tol` of the target,
or warns that it could not, and the dependence runs through all sites.
`"rank"` reaches the same correlation by changing few sites, so a few sites
with low or high effects carry the dependence. With a target above about 0.5
in absolute value it starts from the sorted order, and the result is an almost
exact ordering in which a few sites at the two ends are reversed. Its search
is also the slowest. With 1,000 sites one data set takes many seconds with
`"rank"` and about one second with `"hybrid"`. `"copula"` suits a study in
which the correlation should vary between data sets, as it does between
samples from one population. A relation that is limited to one tail of the
effects, or one that changes direction, is outside what the three methods
model and needs a user-supplied function.

Two settings of the hybrid method leave the rank correlation to chance. With
`rank_corr = 0` it keeps the order of the standard errors, and with
`hybrid_polish = "none"` it stops after the copula draw.
`realized_rank_corr()` shows where a data set ended up.

## Residual and marginal correlation

With site-level covariates (see `vignette("effect-distributions")`) the site
effect is $\tau_j = \tau + x_j'\beta + \sigma_\tau z_j$, and the dependence
step pairs the standard errors with the residual part $z_j$. The target
applies to the residual correlation, between `z_j` and the standard errors.
The marginal correlation, between `tau_j` and the standard errors, is not set
by the design. In the next example the last 50 of 100 sites are urban, and the
effects of urban sites are larger by 0.3 on average.

```{r covariate}
sites <- data.frame(urban = rep(0:1, each = 50))
dat_cov <- sim_multisite(
  J = 100, formula = ~urban, beta = 0.3, data = sites,
  dependence = "hybrid", rank_corr = 0.4, seed = 1
)
realized_rank_corr(dat_cov, on = "residual")
realized_rank_corr(dat_cov, on = "marginal")
```

The residual correlation is 0.400, on target, and the marginal correlation is
0.249. The covariate part of the effect is generated without regard to the
standard errors, which tends to weaken the correlation. In one data set the
marginal correlation also depends on how the covariate happens to line up with
the standard errors. It is the correlation that matters for an analysis that
leaves the covariate out. Without a covariate the two correlations are equal.
The rank correlation in the header is the residual one, and `summary()` prints
both. `plot_dependence()` draws the residual relation, and the marginal one
with `by_residual = FALSE`.

## A user-supplied dependence function

`dependence_fn` replaces the pairing rule of the method named in `dependence`
with a function of your own. With `dependence = "none"` the function is not
used. It is called with three arguments.

- `z_j`: the standardized site effects.
- `se2_j`: the sampling variances, in the order in which they were generated.
- `target`: the value of `rank_corr`, or of `pearson_corr` when
  `dependence = "copula"`.

It must return a list with two elements. `perm` is a permutation of `1:J`, in
which `perm[i]` is the position of the sampling variance that site `i`
receives. `se2_j` is the input `se2_j[perm]`. The package applies `perm` to the
standard errors and the site sizes as well, and stops with an error if the
returned values are not a reordering of the input. The function below ignores
`target`. It gives the largest sampling variances to the sites whose effects
are furthest from the mean in either direction.

```{r custom, fig.cap = "The sampling variances rise with the distance of the site effect from the mean, in both directions."}
by_abs_effect <- function(z_j, se2_j, target) {
  perm <- integer(length(z_j))
  perm[order(abs(z_j))] <- order(se2_j)
  list(se2_j = se2_j[perm], perm = perm)
}
dat_fn <- sim_multisite(
  J = 100, dependence = "rank", dependence_fn = by_abs_effect, seed = 1
)
plot_dependence(dat_fn)
```

`plot_dependence()` draws the sampling variances against the standardized site
effects, with a smooth curve and its bootstrap band. The subtitle gives the
rank correlation, 0.151, and no target. A rank correlation does not describe a
relation of this form. The package does not know what a user-supplied function
aims at, so the header and `summary()` still compare the realized rank
correlation with `rank_corr`.
